questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the dual legitimacy of a semi-presidential system
questions.stem: Planning file note, 1 March: the mayor points out that the president is chosen by the people while the prime minister depends on parliament; what does that arrangement produce?

options.text: It produces dual legitimacy, since the head of state and the head of government hold separate popular and parliamentary mandates.
It produces a single unified mandate, since the president and prime minister together form one electoral mandate.
options.misconception: collapses two mandates into one

options.text: It produces a parliamentary system, because the prime minister's dependence outranks the president's election.
options.misconception: ranks one source of legitimacy above the other

options.text: It produces a presidential system, because direct election of the head of state dominates the arrangement.
options.misconception: ignores the parliamentary element of dual legitimacy

questions.explanation: Dual legitimacy means the head of state and head of government each hold their own authority, one popular and one parliamentary. A single mandate or ranking of the two sources misdescribes it.
questions.hint: Ask where each office draws its authority from.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the constructive condition on a no-confidence vote
questions.stem: Memo to the file, 2 March: a vote of no confidence fails, but a second vote succeeds when the opposition presents an alternative cabinet; what does this outcome demonstrate?

options.text: It demonstrates that a government facing two votes of no confidence is dissolved automatically by the constitution.
options.misconception: confuses defeat in the chamber with automatic dissolution

options.text: It demonstrates the constructive condition: defeat requires a nominated alternative, and success on the second vote forces the government to resign.
It demonstrates that the first vote was void, so only the second vote counted towards the government's survival.

options.misconception: assumes the resignation obligation is merely advisory

questions.explanation: Constructive no-confidence requires a nominated alternative cabinet; once it passes the government must resign. Automatic dissolution, a void first vote and optional resignation misstate it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how cohabitation operates and what it demands of both offices
questions.stem: Internal desk memo, 4 March: the mayor asks why a president and a prime minister from opposing parties can still govern together; explain how cohabitation works and what it demands of each office.

answer.exemplar: Cohabitation occurs when the directly elected president and the parliamentary majority supporting the prime minister come from opposing parties or blocs. The president then retains powers that do not require prime ministerial agreement, such as appointing a prime minister, dissolving parliament or calling a referendum, while the government retains control of ordinary policy and the legislature. Routine government still functions because ministers remain responsible to parliament rather than to the president, but the arrangement demands restraint on both sides: the president avoids using reserve powers for ordinary policy, and the prime minister does not treat the presidency as a rival government.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of cohabitation and its demands on both offices. A strong answer names the reserved powers, the government's ordinary competence and the mutual restraint required.
questions.hint: Separate reserved powers from ordinary government business.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish collective from individual ministerial responsibility

stimulus.body: The report distinguishes two kinds of accountability for ministers. options.misconception: restricts individual questioning to collective policy questions

It shows that collective responsibility applies to ministers and individual responsibility to senior officials.

questions.topic: The semi-presidential trap as a claim
questions.learningObjective: Characterise the argument that the semi-presidential system is a trap

stimulus.body: A briefing note argues that the semi-presidential arrangement is prone to a particular pathology: when the president and the parliamentary majority are from opposing parties, each side may deny the other the ability to govern, producing paralysis over ordinary policy. The note adds that this outcome is not a legal necessity, because the constitution permits collaboration and the reserve powers are used sparingly in practice.

questions.stem: Working file memo, 7 March: on the strength of the extract, which option best describes the argument being made?

options.text: The note claims that the system is legally rigged so that neither side can ever govern.
options.misconception: mistakes a political tendency for a legal impossibility

options.text: The note claims a structural risk of paralysis that careful practice can avoid or limit.
The note claims that reserve powers are routinely used to bypass the parliamentary majority.
options.misconception: asserts routine use of reserve powers the note denies

options.text: The note claims that the pathology disappears whenever the president and majority agree.
options.misconception: assumes the risk vanishes with shared party control

questions.explanation: The note describes a structural risk of paralysis under divided support and denies legal necessity. Legal impossibility, routine reserve-power use and vanished risk each overstate the argument.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is legal or political in character.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how counter-signature can bring down a government
questions.stem: Memo, 8 March: the mayor asks how a refusal to counter-sign an order can bring down a government; explain how ministerial counter-signature works and why it carries that risk.

answer.exemplar: Counter-signature means that an order or decision of the government must be signed by the ministers responsible for it, in addition to the head of government, so that the act is jointly attributable. Because signature is a legal act with political consequences, a minister who believes an order is unlawful may withhold it. If enough ministers refuse, the instrument cannot issue, the government appears unable to govern, and ministers who refuse may force the head of government to resign or face a no-confidence motion. The mechanism therefore links a legal competence to a political weapon.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written explanation linking counter-signature to the fall of governments. A strong answer describes the joint signature requirement and how withholding it becomes a political weapon.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when a required signature is withheld.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the parties must operate during divided support
questions.stem: Note in the file, 12 March: the mayor asks what happens to a reform bill during cohabitation when the president's party controls the assembly; explain how the parties must then work.

answer.exemplar: During cohabitation the government retains the initiative on ordinary policy because it still enjoys the confidence of the assembly, but every bill it proposes may face a hostile majority in the legislature. Because the president is not obliged to sign ordinary legislation, the president cannot stop a bill that the assembly has passed. The government therefore has to carry reforms through the assembly itself, which means negotiation, compromise and sometimes seeking support beyond its own bloc, while the president has to choose between using reserve powers that would damage the reform and remaining a largely ceremonial figure during the term.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks how the parties operate under divided support. A strong answer explains that the government must build majorities while the president weighs reserve powers against their cost.
questions.hint: Think about who must now find the votes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the constitutional problem of allowing refusal to sign
questions.stem: Internal desk memo, 16 March: a proposal would let two named ministers refuse to sign a disputed order and refers the matter to a committee; explain what constitutional problem that creates.

answer.exemplar: Refusing to sign is normally an act of collective responsibility rather than an individual objection, because signature makes the order jointly attributable to the ministers who sign it. If ministers may withhold signature on grounds of personal disagreement, the government loses the ability to act, and the dispute becomes about the confidence of the chamber rather than about the legal quality of the order. A committee reference would therefore replace a political confidence mechanism with a legal review, allowing a small group of ministers to block the executive by procedural means, and leaving unclear whether the signatories or the dissenting ministers bear responsibility for the consequences.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written analysis of the problem a refusal-to-sign power would create. A strong answer connects joint signature, collective responsibility and the shift from confidence to legal review.
questions.hint: Think about who becomes responsible for an unsigned order.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the convention that gives a cohabiting president a chance
questions.stem: Memo, 20 March: the mayor asks why, during cohabitation, a president who is disliked by the majority is still obliged to give the government a real chance; explain how that duty works.

answer.exemplar: Under cohabitation the president retains formal powers that do not depend on the prime minister, including appointing the prime minister, dissolving the legislature and calling a referendum, and these give the office a genuine capacity to obstruct. The convention that gives the government a real chance requires the president to delay those powers and to refrain from using them to reverse ordinary government policy or to force a premature election that the president's own side would welcome. Because the convention has no legal sanction, its strength depends on political calculation: a president who ignores it risks isolating the office and being described as a usurper, and a government that ignores it risks a deadlock that neither side wants.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written explanation of the convention giving a cohabiting president a chance to govern. A strong answer links reserved powers, the lack of legal sanction and the politics of restraint.
questions.hint: Think about what the president gives up in practice.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare refusal of signature with removal by the legislature
questions.stem: Note in the file, 24 March: the mayor asks how a rule allowing ministers to refuse signature differs from a rule allowing the legislature to remove a minister; explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: Refusal of signature and removal by the legislature operate on different levels and at different moments. Signature is part of the act of government, so a minister who refuses it withholds the means by which a policy becomes effective, and if enough ministers do so the government cannot govern and must seek the confidence of the chamber. Removal by the legislature, by contrast, is a verdict on the government as a whole and operates only after the chamber has moved against it, normally through a no-confidence motion. The first instrument is therefore a block on execution, individual in use and immediate in effect; the second is a sanction for the government's continuing in office.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written comparison of refusal of signature and legislative removal. A strong answer distinguishes an immediate block on execution from a verdict on the government's continued tenure.
questions.hint: Compare what each instrument blocks or ends.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why divided support unsettles the institutions
questions.stem: Internal desk memo, 28 March: the mayor asks why cohabitation is often described as a period of institutional discomfort; explain what makes it uncomfortable for both sides.

answer.exemplar: Cohabitation is uncomfortable because neither office can act as if it were the sole source of authority. The president holds a direct popular mandate and retains the reserve powers of appointment, dissolution and referendum, so the government can never be sure of the president's silence; the government, meanwhile, controls ordinary policy and the legislature, so the president cannot make a credible claim to govern. Each side therefore suspects the other of intending to use its position to undo the other, and the constant possibility of an early election or a referendum makes even routine decisions contested. Neither side, however, has a decisive advantage, so the arrangement usually settles into a working division of labour rather than a permanent crisis.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks why divided support unsettles the institutions. A strong answer identifies mutual suspicion about reserved powers and the contestation of routine decisions.
questions.hint: Think about what each side fears the other will do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the trade-off between speed and ministerial control
questions.stem: Memo, 1 April: the mayor asks how the requirement that orders be counter-signed affects the balance between speed and ministerial control; explain how the two are traded off.

answer.exemplar: Counter-signature ties the legal effectiveness of an order to the consent of the minister responsible for it. This buys a form of individual accountability, because the minister who signs answers for the measure, but it also creates a veto point inside the executive, since a single minister can withhold signature and stop the instrument from issuing. Reformers worried about delays therefore tend to widen the circle of required signatures or to permit orders to take effect provisionally, while ministers worried about accountability tend to insist on the strict form. Neither concern can be removed without losing something real: without signatures the executive becomes unaccountable, and without an effective signature requirement the individual minister's responsibility is largely formal.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of the trade-off between speed and ministerial control. A strong answer links counter-signature to individual accountability and delay, and to the cost of remedies.
questions.hint: Ask what is lost when signatures are relaxed or required.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why dissolution is treated as exceptional under divided support
questions.stem: Note in the file, 5 April: the mayor asks why the president's dissolution power is treated differently during cohabitation from the president's ordinary powers; explain the distinction.

answer.exemplar: The president of a semi-presidential system normally holds a reserve power to dissolve the legislature and call a new election, which exists so that the office can resolve a deadlock between the two mandates. Under cohabitation, that power becomes politically explosive, because the president's own side stands to gain from an early election while the government's side treats it as a device to overturn a legislature that has just refused to support it. The convention that the president give the government a real chance therefore operates most strongly here: the president is expected to exhaust ordinary measures, such as appointing a prime minister who will accept the programme or seeking an understanding through the legislature, before turning to dissolution. The power remains legally intact, but its use is expected to be exceptional and last.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written explanation of why dissolution is exceptional under divided support. A strong answer contrasts the reserve power with ordinary measures and with the political cost of using it.
questions.hint: Think about who benefits from an early election.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out mechanisms that could restrain a refusal to sign
questions.stem: Internal desk memo, 9 April: the mayor asks how a refusal to counter-sign could be checked and limited; explain the mechanisms that might restrain such a refusal.

answer.exemplar: Any workable restraint must combine a check on the legality of the refusal with a check on its political use. A legal check would allow the prime minister or the council of ministers to test whether the refusal rests on a genuine legal objection to the order or merely on a disagreement with its policy, and to put that question before an independent body where the case is arguable. A political check would work through collective responsibility itself, since ministers who obstruct the government's programme risk losing their own seat, and through a rule that refusal must be declared publicly with reasons, which exposes obstruction to the chamber. Critics add that no such device is foolproof, because a minister able to argue a technical point in good faith can still immobilise the executive for as long as the argument lasts.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of mechanisms restraining a refusal to sign. A strong answer combines a legal test of the ground with political exposure and notes safeguards' limits.
questions.hint: Think about checking the ground and the consequences.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out the channels a cohabiting president retains
questions.stem: Memo, 13 April: the mayor asks why a president in cohabitation can still shape policy without acting as head of government; explain the channels that remain open.

answer.exemplar: Several channels remain open to a cohabiting president who cannot command the legislature. Appointments to senior posts, the choice of a prime minister, the dissolution power and the ability to convene or address the nation all remain his, and each shapes the conditions under which the government operates without any instruction from him. Informal meetings with ministers, party leaders and the head of state are a further route, because the president's own following in the chamber can change the government's arithmetic even though the majority is hostile. The importance of these channels lies in their restraint as much as their reach, since the constitution makes the president responsible for the general functioning of the institutions but leaves ordinary policy to the government, and a president who treats informal meetings as policy-making quickly loses the acceptance that makes those meetings useful.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of the channels a cohabiting president retains. A strong answer lists reserved powers and informal routes, and separates them from ordinary policy-making.
questions.hint: Think about appointment, address and the legislature's arithmetic.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare design options for counter-signature rules
questions.stem: Note in the file, 17 April: the mayor asks how a rule requiring counter-signature for routine orders could be improved to protect ministers without slowing government; explain the design options.

answer.exemplar: Any improvement has to answer the two questions the rule raises: how much delay the requirement causes, and how easily a minister can be made to carry responsibility for a measure he opposed. Several designs are open. The circle of required signatures can be narrowed so that only orders with budgetary or regulatory effect need more than the prime minister's signature. A duty to concur can be replaced by a duty to notify, so that an objecting minister must state his objection in writing but the order proceeds unless the objection is sustained on an objective test, such as a finding that the order exceeds the minister's statutory powers or requires expenditure that has not been approved. Time limits can be attached to any challenge, so that an objection unresolved after a fixed period lapses. Each design trades some protection against some speed, and none removes the political risk that a determined group of ministers can immobilise the executive.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written comparison of counter-signature designs. A strong answer weighs narrower signature circles, notice over concurrence, objective tests and time limits against each other.
questions.hint: Weigh delay against protection for each option.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why early elections suit both sides of a cohabitation
questions.stem: Internal desk memo, 21 April: the mayor asks why early elections are the usual way cohabitation ends; explain what makes an early election attractive to both sides.

answer.exemplar: An early election is attractive to both sides because it resolves the conflict by returning the decision to the electorate, where the president's mandate has its origin, and because it lets each side present the disagreement as a verdict on the government rather than as an internal contest. The president's side gains the chance to convert a hostile legislature into a fresh one; the government's side gains the chance to argue that it was the president's obstruction, and not the government's record, that caused the disorder, and to seek a fresh majority at a time of its choosing. Governments that are confident in their record therefore tend to resist dissolution, while presidents whose parliamentary position has become untenable tend to seek it, and the risk of a snap poll deters both from patterns of behaviour that would otherwise be difficult to defend.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written explanation of why an early election suits both sides. A strong answer shows how each turns the dissolution power into an advantage and notes the deterrent effect.
questions.hint: Think about what each side gains from the electorate judging.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the total period for a compatibility procedure
questions.stem: Memo for the committee, 22 April: the standing orders give a compatibility declaration 18 days to be lodged and 12 days for the committee to report, with a further 6 days for the chamber to pronounce; how many days elapse in total?
questions.explanation: The stages run 18 days to lodge, 12 for the committee report and 6 for the pronouncement, giving 36 days. Treating them as alternatives, or omitting the reporting stage, understates the period.
questions.hint: Add all three stages in the rule.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the complementarity of the two ministerial duties

stimulus.body: The review states that individual ministerial responsibility is not a substitute for collective responsibility but a complement to it, and that the legislature may examine a minister on his own acts even where the cabinet as a whole has given him its confidence. It adds that the complementarity works in both directions, because a minister who has been found at fault individually may still be expected to defend the government's policy in the chamber unless his conduct is incompatible with his membership of the government.

questions.stem: Planning note, 23 April: on the strength of the extract, which option best captures the position on individual responsibility?

options.text: It runs alongside collective responsibility, so individual examination and collective defence continue together.
It replaces collective responsibility, so a minister examined individually no longer owes collective loyalty.
options.misconception: treats individual scrutiny as displacing collective defence

options.text: It is limited to criminal matters, so a minister is examined individually only for offences.
options.misconception: restricts individual examination to criminal cases

options.text: It depends on the government first questioning the minister, so silence protects him from examination.
options.misconception: makes government silence a shield from individual scrutiny

questions.explanation: The review presents individual and collective responsibility as complements operating at once, in both directions. Replacement, a criminal-only limit and protection by silence each misread it.
questions.hint: Ask whether one duty displaces the other.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The semi-presidential trap as a claim
questions.learningObjective: State the conditional conclusion reached about the trap

stimulus.body: A working paper sets out four ways in which the claim of a semi-presidential trap can be weakened: by showing that the trap requires specific partisan conditions rather than the constitutional rules themselves, by showing that the reserve devices are seldom used, by showing that divided governments have produced durable policy, and by showing that comparable conflicts in systems without a reserve dissolution power were resolved without paralysis. It concludes that the claim is best understood as a conditional risk rather than a structural defect.

questions.stem: Working file memo, 24 April: on the strength of the extract, which option best describes the paper's conclusion?

options.text: The paper concludes that the trap claim is unfounded, since every listed line of argument fails.
options.misconception: turns a conditional conclusion into a wholesale dismissal

options.text: The paper concludes that the trap is a conditional risk rather than an inherent structural defect.
The paper concludes that the trap is a structural defect, since reserve devices are rarely used.
options.misconception: reverses the paper's own conclusion

options.text: The paper concludes that comparisons with systems lacking dissolution powers are irrelevant.
options.misconception: dismisses one of the paper's own arguments

questions.explanation: The paper lands on a conditional reading, in which the risk arises from partisan conditions rather than from constitutional rules. Wholesale dismissal, reversal and dismissed comparisons misread it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the risk is stated as structural or conditional.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how joint attribution and the capacity to govern are balanced
questions.stem: Memo, 25 April: the mayor asks how the requirement that ministers sign the acts of government could be reconciled with the need for a government to be able to act; explain the way the two requirements are balanced.

answer.exemplar: The two requirements are reconciled by accepting that some acts cannot be made jointly attributable without making government unworkable, and by designing the exception accordingly. Acts of the government proper, those concerning the general running of the country, are made subject to counter-signature because they carry the whole authority of the executive and are most in need of collective responsibility. Personal acts of the head of government, such as appointing a minister or dissolving the legislature, are left to him alone, since attaching ministerial signatures to them would either dilute the responsibility of the president or make his own choices hostage to colleagues. Between the two lies a contested zone, covering appointments, spending and external commitments, where the choice between collective signature and individual authority is not settled by principle but by the practice and conventions of each system.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of how joint attribution and the capacity to govern are balanced. A strong answer separates acts of government from personal acts and identifies the contested zone between them.
questions.hint: Separate acts of government from personal acts of the president.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the relationship between the two elections
questions.stem: Site note, 26 April: the mayor asks how the two elections in a semi-presidential system relate to each other; what relationship do they have?

options.text: They are held together, so that a single vote settles both the presidency and the assembly.
options.misconception: conflates two separate mandates into one ballot

options.text: The earlier election binds the later one, so the president's vote ratifies the assembly's choice.
options.misconception: invents a ratification sequence between the elections

options.text: The legislative election settles the government, while the presidential election merely confirms it.
options.misconception: reduces the presidential election to a formality

options.text: They are separate, so each mandate is returned on its own and may point in different directions.

questions.explanation: The two elections return the mandates independently, so each office draws authority from a separate ballot and results may diverge. A joint vote, ratification and confirmatory votes misdescribe it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two ballots can be decided separately.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Determine the outcome of a bare majority of the chamber
questions.stem: Briefing memo, 27 April: a chamber of 250 records 126 votes for a no-confidence motion naming an alternative cabinet and 120 votes against, with 4 abstentions; what follows?

options.text: The motion carried, because 126 is more than half of 250 members, so the government must resign.
The motion failed, because abstentions reduce the number needed to a simple majority of those voting.
options.misconception: adjusts the threshold to the votes actually cast

options.text: The motion failed, because a no-confidence motion needs a two-thirds majority of the membership.
options.misconception: invents a two-thirds threshold

options.text: The motion is void, because an alternative cabinet must be approved by the outgoing prime minister first.
options.misconception: invents an approval step the log does not mention

questions.explanation: 126 of 250 is a simple majority of the chamber, so with a named alternative the motion carried and the government must resign. Adjusting the threshold, a two-thirds rule and an approval step misread it.
questions.hint: Check the votes for against half the membership.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why collective defence continues after a confidence defeat
questions.stem: File memo, 28 April: the mayor asks why a government that has lost a confidence vote may still be asked to defend its policy in the chamber; explain the reasoning.

options.text: Because the members of a government that has lost a vote are automatically released from their duties.
options.misconception: assumes defeat releases ministers from collective defence

options.text: Because collective responsibility binds ministers to the government's decisions regardless of the vote's outcome.
Because the legislature loses its authority to question ministers once it has voted against them.
options.misconception: strips the legislature of its questioning power

options.text: Because the prime minister may instruct dissenting ministers to defend the policy anyway.
options.misconception: reduces collective defence to a command from one office

questions.explanation: Collective responsibility binds ministers to the government's decisions whatever the chamber decided, so the defence continues. Automatic release, questioning bars and a prime-ministerial command misdescribe it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the vote changes what ministers owe.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out the resolutions open to a presidential deadlock
questions.stem: Note in the file, 29 April: the mayor asks what happens to the parliamentary majority when a president and government disagree and neither will move; explain the possible resolutions and their costs.

answer.exemplar: When the president and the parliamentary majority are locked in conflict, three routes are usually available, and each has a cost the others avoid. The president may use a reserve power, such as appointing a prime minister who will carry the programme or dissolving the legislature, which shows the office has real weight but invites the accusation that the presidency is taking over the government and usually produces an early election. The government may absorb the conflict and govern on the contested area as far as the assembly allows, which preserves stability but invites the criticism that a president has been ignored while the country is realigned around government policy. The two sides may also reach an accommodation through a period of shared or non-contested measures, which avoids both costs but produces a period in which neither office governs the disputed subject and the disagreement returns when the accommodation lapses.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of the resolutions open to a deadlock and their costs. A strong answer presents the reserve-power and accommodation routes and the price of each.
questions.hint: Ask what each way out costs the side that chooses it.
